title: MergeRec: Model Merging for Data-Isolated Cross-Domain Sequential Recommendation

problem.claim: Domain-specific recommender systems struggle to generalize across multiple domains, while data-isolated settings prohibit sharing raw user interaction data across domains.

gap.claim: Existing cross-domain sequential recommendation approaches rely on overlapping users or items, or make unrealistic assumptions that ignore privacy constraints.

contributions.claim: MergeRec is a model-merging framework for data-isolated cross-domain sequential recommendation.
The framework combines merging initialization, pseudo-user data construction, and collaborative merging optimization.
Pseudo-user data treats each item as a virtual sequence in each domain to synthesize training samples without real user interactions.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors present MergeRec as a new framework based on model merging and introduce a new problem setting called data-isolated cross-domain sequential recommendation.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that extensive experiments show MergeRec preserves the strengths of the original models and enhances generalizability to unseen domains.
The authors report that MergeRec achieves average improvements of up to 17.21% in Recall@10 over conventional model merging methods.

narrative_sequence.summary: Domain-specific recommendation models have difficulty generalizing across domains, and existing cross-domain methods have overlap and privacy limitations.
The work defines data-isolated cross-domain sequential recommendation and proposes MergeRec, with initialization, pseudo-user construction, and collaborative merging optimization.
MergeRec uses training-free model merging, virtual item sequences for pseudo-user data, and a joint recommendation-distillation objective.
The authors report improved generalizability and up to 17.21% average Recall@10 improvement over conventional model merging methods.

source_observation.claim: Pseudo-user data can be synthesized from item-based virtual sequences when real user interactions cannot be shared.

interpretation.claim: Structured proxies may enable cross-domain training while preserving data isolation.

application.claim: Consider privacy-preserving synthetic interaction representations when designing systems across isolated data owners.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish whether the synthesized sequences preserve all information needed for reliable recommendation across domains.

source_observation.claim: The optimization combines recommendation loss with distillation loss from fine-tuned source models.

interpretation.claim: Jointly preserving task performance and source-model collaborative signals may improve merged-model generalization.

application.claim: Use multi-objective optimization when merging specialized models that must retain both target-task behavior and source-model knowledge.

exception.claim: The abstract does not specify how the loss terms are weighted or when the trade-off is beneficial.

unknowns: Datasets, domain characteristics, and evaluation protocols are unspecified.
Baseline configurations and statistical significance of the reported improvements are unspecified.
The abstract does not provide ablations, computational costs, or privacy guarantees.
